articles.title: Amazon Bedrock Agents Orchestrating Google ADK over A2A
articles.excerpt: This article explains how to build and test a cross-cloud currency agent. An Amazon Bedrock master agent, built with Strands Agents and hosted on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime in AWS us-east-1, del…
articles.body: This article explains how to build and test a cross-cloud currency agent. An Amazon Bedrock master agent , built with Strands Agents and hosted on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime in AWS us-east-1 , delegates to a Google ADK worker on GCP Cloud Run in us-central1 over A2A v1.0 . The master cross-checks the worker against an MCP exchange-rate tool and measures the latency, reliability, and failure behavior of cross-cloud verification. What is this project trying to do? Most Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol demos stop at "look, the HTTP 200 OK request succeeded." That is a smoke test, not an interoperability benchmark. This project goes further: the Bedrock master owns the user interaction and benchmark policy.

articles.title: NASA launched this spacecraft to save a satellite. Now, it needs saving too
articles.excerpt: NASA launched the Swift Boost mission earlier this month to try and save one of its aging science observatories, but the rescue spacecraft is now experiencing control issues.
articles.body: Things aren't going so well for NASA's latest satellite rescue mission. NASA launched the Swift Boost mission on July 3, sending a specialized spacecraft to low Earth orbit on the final flight of Northrop Grumman's air-launched Pegasus XL rocket. The spacecraft is called LINK and was built by Arizona-based Katalyst Space Technologies. LINK was sent to orbit to try and link up with NASA's Swift observatory , a highly successful scientific satellite designed to search for gamma-ray bursts , some of the most energetic events in the universe. But it looks like just a few weeks after launch, LINK is experiencing some issues.

articles.excerpt: A genuinely pocket-sized smart telescope
articles.body: The best smart telescopes have transformed astrophotography over the past few years, combining small telescope optics and automated mounts with dashcam-style camera sensors and image-processing software. The result? Compact devices that can be controlled entirely from a smartphone. Impressively, the DwarfLab Dwarf Mini pushes that concept even further. Roughly the size of a thick paperback book, it’s one of the smallest smart telescopes yet produced — tiny enough to fit in a jacket pocket while still capable of imaging nebulae, star clusters, the moon and even sunspots. It's also one of the best telescopes for beginners . Positioned below the larger Dwarf 3 in DwarfLab’s lineup, the Mini sacrifices aperture and resolution for portability.

articles.title: 'The Ark' creator Dean Devlin talks season 3's enormous mystery box and sci-fi surprises (interview)
articles.excerpt: "We went wildly over budget and just made the biggest craziest season we could possible imagine."
articles.body: SYFY’s optimistic space opera series, " The Ark ," embarks upon its third thrilling season today, occupying a unique entertainment spot as the only weekly scripted sci-fi series currently on regular broadcast television. With an impressive creative resume featuring executive producers Dean Devlin ("Stargate," "Independence Day") and Jonathan Glassner ("Stargate SG-1") and a hopeful premise about humanity’s search for a new home amid the stars, it’s a refreshing show perfect for a laidback, summertime watch. Season 3 delivers more dangerous exoplanets inhabited by ravenous toothy monsters, the mystery of an alien stone tablet, and Captain Sharon Garnet’s Ark One searching for long-lost colonists. We caught up with Devlin to find out more about this third outing.

articles.body: SpaceX's Starship Version 3 floats on the Indian Ocean on July 28, 2026, days after splashing down on the vehicle's Flight Test 13 on July 24. (Image credit: SpaceX via X) SpaceX's Starship V3 looks absolutely seaworthy in this new photo taken days after its most recent flight test. What is it? SpaceX launched its Starship vehicle on July 24, sending the 408-foot-tall (124-meter) Starship Version 3 (V3) rocket on a suborbital trajectory that saw the rocket's upper stage make its softest splashdown yet . In fact, the landing was so smooth that Starship is still floating off the coast of Western Australia.

articles.title: On this day in space! July 29, 1982: Soviet Salyut 6 space station falls to Earth
articles.excerpt: On July 29, 1982, the Salyut 6 space station fell out of space and safely burned up in Earth's atmosphere along the way. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On July 29, 1982, the Salyut 6 space station fell out of space and safely burned up in Earth's atmosphere along the way. Salyut 6 was the eighth space station the Soviet Union had built for its Salyut program . It spent almost five years in orbit and supported five different crewed cosmonaut missions. While aboard Salyut 6, those cosmonauts made astronomical observations and studied the effects of spaceflight on the human body . Though the aging space station was still considered fully functional in 1982, a mold problem in the crew quarters led the Soviets to abandon the orbiting lab. They intentionally sent it plunging toward Earth, where it would burn up in the atmosphere before hitting the ground.
